stops.title: Scout six of twelve pads.
stops.silver: A table keeps one number per state and learns each one on its own. Fine for the island's 48 squares. Hopeless when there are more states than you could ever visit, which is Silver's whole problem in this lecture.
stops.do: Twelve pads lie in a row, each hiding a danger number. Walk into a ring with WASD and press F (Interact) to read it. You get 6 reads; each costs a small hit and can be off by 1.
stops.predict: Before you start, choose which 6 pads will tell your team the most about all 12.
stops.saw: Each read landed on its own pad and nowhere else, so half the strip is still blank. That is Silver's problem at toy size: your budget is smaller than the number of states. In a real game the gap is not 6 against 12. It is a handful against more states than there are atoms.
stops.agent: An agent meets a conversation it has never seen in every session. A notebook with one stored answer per conversation would be blank on every page that matters.

stops.title: Guess which map wins after six calls.
stops.silver: The callout idea. Describe each state by a few features, give each a weight, add them up. Now one lesson moves the estimate for every state that shares those features, the way one "mid is hot" warns the team about a whole area.
stops.do: Your 6 reads fed three maps: EXACT keeps 12 numbers, THIRDS keeps 3, ONE WORD keeps 1. A question floats in front of you. Answer with left click, right click or melee, then read the truth and each map's numbers under the pads.
stops.predict: Commit to the map you think sits closest to the truth on all 12 pads after only 6 reads.
stops.saw: EXACT knows the pads you stepped on and writes 0 on the rest. A table cannot guess where it has not been. THIRDS writes its third's average on all four pads, so one read reached four places. That spreading is called generalisation, and it is usually why THIRDS wins this early.
stops.agent: A language model answers a prompt it never saw by how much it looks like prompts it did see. Same spreading, much bigger map.

stops.title: Predict 60 calls, then press F.
stops.silver: Fire the oracle. Nobody tells you a state's true value, so you use the return you actually saw. Each return is right on average and noisy every time, so you average them.
stops.do: The team adds 54 calls, every pad read 4 or 5 times. Answer two questions with the mouse buttons or melee, then press F to bring the calls in and read the table on the right.
stops.predict: Decide which map will be closest after 60 calls, and whether EXACT, which averages each pad's reads, will be exactly right.
stops.saw: With every pad visited, EXACT wins. Its miss is small, not zero: each pad's number is an average of a few reads, each off by up to 1. That is lecture 4's Monte Carlo estimate. Notice how little THIRDS and ONE WORD moved from 6 calls to 60. And EXACT is the same method with one group per pad: a table is the special case with one feature per state.

stops.title: Find where THIRDS stays wrong.
stops.silver: Silver's warning: an approximator may be unable to represent the true values at all, however much experience it gets. More scouting cannot fix a map that has no word for what you found.
stops.do: Picture scouting forever, every pad read endlessly. Answer two questions with left click, right click or melee, then read the forever column on the right and the numbers under the pads.
stops.predict: Choose which maps can never get every pad right, and on which pad THIRDS stays most wrong.
stops.saw: With endless reads EXACT reaches 0. THIRDS stops at 1.99 and ONE WORD at 3.39. Most of THIRDS' miss is pad 10, a 9 among 1s and 2s that it calls 3.25, and the same average drags pad 12 up. A coarse map learns fast and has a floor. Scouting forever does not get you under it.
stops.agent: When two prompts look alike to a model but need different answers, it gives both the same confident answer. That is THIRDS calling pad 10 a 3.25 because its neighbours are calm.

stops.title: Give one pad its own number.
stops.silver: Good features can make the true value far easier to learn. Choosing them is where your knowledge goes in, and Silver says so plainly.
stops.do: Walk into one pad's ring and press F (Interact). That pad gets its own number on top of THIRDS, a map of 4 numbers. Answer one question with the mouse buttons or melee, then read the YOURS row on the right.
stops.predict: Once your pad is picked, commit to how far it will pull THIRDS' forever miss down from 1.99.
stops.saw: One pad matters far more than the rest. Split off pad 10 and the floor drops from 1.99 to 0.55, with just 4 numbers. Pick any other pad and it stays between 1.85 and 1.99, because that pad already fit its group. Where you put the feature mattered more than how many you had. Choosing the description is most of the work.

stops.title: Read the debrief.
stops.silver: With linear features you can skip the nudging. Solve once over all your experience and the best weights fall out. The size of that calculation depends on the number of features, not the number of states.
stops.do: Nothing to press. Read the three lines on the left and your prediction score.
stops.predict: Before you read, say in one sentence what the three maps had in common and what made them differ.
stops.saw: All three maps were the same method: average the calls in each group. For features that are on in one group and off everywhere else, that average is exactly the least-squares answer. Only the grouping differed. This was value function approximation at its mildest, fixed hand-made groups and plain averages. A neural network learns its own features, and that is where the guarantees thin out.
stops.agent: A value head on a language-model agent reads the whole conversation and learns its own callouts instead of being handed them.
